metric.dependency_simplicity.description: Assessment of language-level dependency semantics for Rust, independent of Cargo ecosystem maturity (which belongs to Ecosystem evaluation).
observations: Rust programs reviewed under /quidra-benchmark/template/programs/rust/micro (mb00.rs through mb11.rs) are self-contained, relying only on the Rust standard library (std::collections, std::io, std::fmt, etc.) with no external crate dependencies required for core micro-benchmark logic.

Rust's module system (mod, use, pub) provides explicit, unambiguous dependency declaration at the language level: every external symbol used must be explicitly brought into scope via use, and crate dependencies are declared once in Cargo.toml with semantic versioning enforced by Cargo.lock rather than manual header/linker bookkeeping.

No global mutable namespace pollution: Rust has no implicit global includes or preprocessor-based conditional dependency inclusion (unlike C/C++ #include and #ifdef chains), reducing accidental coupling.

Cargo's dependency resolution is deterministic and reproducible via Cargo.lock; Rust has no stable ABI to break, each crate is recompiled from source with monomorphization, and binaries are statically linked by default, so what you use is what you link.

Feature flags (Cargo features) allow fine-grained optional dependency inclusion via Cargo.toml + #[cfg(feature = ...)] keeping unused dependency code out of the final binary without complex build scripting in most cases.

Downside: build scripts (build.rs) and procedural macros can introduce compile-time dependency complexity (e.g. requiring a C toolchain for some sys crates), a real but ecosystem-adjacent concern that only mildly discounts the score.
metric.dependency_simplicity.score_rationale: Rust scores highly (88/100) for dependency simplicity: explicit use imports, no implicit globals, static linking by default, deterministic Cargo.lock resolution, and cfg-gated optional features. Points withheld reflect occasional build-script/proc-macro-induced complexity, a minor language-design wrinkle rather than an ecosystem issue.

metric.portability_design_platform_neutr.description: Assessment of Rust's language/compiler design for platform neutrality, independent of the breadth of currently realized supported platforms (an Ecosystem concern).
observations: Rust's std library is explicitly layered (core/alloc/std) allowing targeting freestanding, no_std, and embedded environments without any language changes -- a first-class, deliberate portability design feature.

The micro-benchmark programs reviewed (mb00.rs-mb11.rs) use only std::collections, std::time, std::fmt and similar platform-neutral APIs with no OS-specific syscalls or inline asm, demonstrating that idiomatic Rust code naturally stays portable.
Cross-compilation is a designed-in compiler feature (rustc --target, cargo build --target) backed by LLVM, letting a single toolchain target many architectures/OSes from one host.
Conditional compilation via #[cfg(target_os = ...)], #[cfg(target_arch = ...)] is a structured, compiler-checked mechanism for platform-specific code paths, rather than textual preprocessor hacks.
Rust has no undefined/implementation-defined ABI reliance for typical safe code; memory layout guarantees (repr(C) opt-in) make FFI/portability explicit and opt-in rather than accidental.
Rust does not mandate a garbage collector or heavyweight managed runtime, so it can target bare-metal and WASM equally well; realized platform breadth itself is scored separately under Ecosystem.
metric.portability_design_platform_neutr.score_rationale: Rust scores very highly (90/100) for portability design: layered std/core/alloc, structured cfg-based conditional compilation, first-class cross-compilation support in the compiler, no mandatory runtime/GC, and opt-in explicit ABI/layout control for FFI. Small deduction reflects that certain std APIs still assume a hosted OS environment by default (no_std requires deliberate opt-out).
